page_title: Job, Site and Payout Tracking for Crews | Robotics Consulting
page_desc: I build tracking systems for small companies where the work happens on-site: construction and renovation, fit-out, installation, service calls. Site-based jobs, expenses, materials and crew payouts — instead of Excel and WhatsApp. Riga, Latvia.
hero_title: Who did what, on which site, and who gets paid — in one system
hero_lead: My name is Arturs Staseluns. I build tracking systems for small companies in Latvia where the work happens on-site: who did what, what they're owed for it, and what's actually left on the site — calculated automatically, not in Excel, WhatsApp and on paper. Launch is free, and so is the first month on your data.
hero_lead_mobile: Arturs Staseluns. I build tracking systems for companies where the work happens on-site: jobs, payouts and expenses instead of Excel and WhatsApp. Launch is free.
concept_auto_sub: The foreman enters the plan before work starts and the actuals once it's done — the office already has the numbers. Fewer mistakes and a lot less time lost.
kpi_1_sub: The same job costs a different amount on different sites — in the demo data, screed rates differ 8x. The system flags anything priced below 60% of your own average rate while the site is still open, not at year-end.
kpi_2_title: You see a cash-flow gap coming

kpi_3_sub: The system sets aside 4–10% of every payout into a reserve — so crews have something to draw on in winter, and people don't look for other work.
kpi_4_sub: Launch is free, and so is the first month on your data. The database lives on your server — export it and leave whenever you want.

problem_body: Companies where the work happens on-site tend to run into the same thing:
problem_body_mobile: Common problems for businesses with crews on-site:
problem_q1: How much you made on a site is only clear at the end — if it's clear at all
problem_q2: Output and crew payouts get calculated by hand, and it's an argument every month
problem_q3: Receipts and expenses come in from sites however they come in — some go missing
problem_q4: Everything lives in the owner's head, so there's no one to delegate to
problem_note: This is exactly what I fix — usually with one system, where data gets entered right where the work happens.
demo_title: You can try the system before paying
demo_lead: Objecty — a CRM for tracking jobs, sites and crew payouts — is already built and deployed on a test server. It's not a mockup or a pitch deck: log in and click around yourself, no form, no waiting. Inside are reports on site profitability, cash flow and rate discipline — answering questions like "where's the real profit," "will there be enough cash next month," and "how much is leaking to below-market rates."
demo_lead_mobile: Objecty is already running on a test server. Not a mockup — log in and click around yourself, no form.
demo_point_1: No form, no signup — opens right away. You'll set up a site, a crew and a work type yourself
demo_point_2: See how payouts get calculated and how that flows into reports — site profitability, cash flow, rate discipline
demo_point_3: Launch takes about a month — exactly the month that's free
demo_shot_caption: The foreman fills in the plan in the morning and the actuals once the work is done — output and payout are calculated automatically.
demo_note: The demo and screenshots are demo data — I don't show real client numbers. The system grew out of screed and flooring, calculated by m² and m³, but work types, units and rates are configurable — roofing, façade work, installation and cleaning fit the same engine. If your bookkeeping isn't built around sites and crews, that's a different system, and I'll say so right away. Objecty doesn't replace accounting: it tracks sites and payouts upstream of it. Connecting to Horizon or Jumis, so you're not entering data twice, is a separate job — price is in the "How much this costs" section.

about_honest: Objecty grew out of Go Gridas — a CRM for a real construction company, where I worked through real sites, real rates and real end-of-month payout disputes. The winter reserve and the underpriced-rate catch weren't my idea — they came from the site. Their rollout is still under way, so the numbers in the screenshots are demo data. That's exactly why the first three Objecty rollouts get a €0 launch instead of the usual €1,500 — it's an open pilot, not an excuse: in exchange I ask for a review and permission to name your company once the system is running.

pricing_why_toggle: Why it's set up this way
pricing_why: Because this isn't the price of development. Development is already paid for: Objecty is built and working — you're deploying a ready system, not commissioning a new one, which is why the base is so low. From there, the price grows with the number of crews not because of the server, but because of volume: more people and sites means more data and more questions from foremen, which I support personally. Every tier is fixed by contract and won't rise unilaterally.

faq_sub: Real questions I get from business owners before their first step.
faq_a1: Honestly: the system doesn't make money on its own — it shows you where you're losing it. On-site that's usually rates below average, unbilled extra work, missing receipts and overpaid output. While you only have a handful of sites, you can still see it. With 50-70 sites a year, you can't — and it only surfaces at year-end, when it's too late to fix. And without numbers you can't delegate: a business can't grow bigger than what the owner can hold in their head.
faq_a2:
The full price table is in "How much this costs" above — here's the short version:
Objecty as-is — €0 launch and the first month on your data, then €250/month for server, updates and support. This isn't the price of development — that's already paid for, and €250 won't rise: the price is fixed by contract.
Payback is easy to check: the system flags line items priced below 60% of your average rate — usually one caught job a month is enough for the subscription to pay for itself.
No mandatory terms: the data is yours, export it and leave any time.
Different work types — launch is €1,500 plus the same €250/month. A standalone automation without the full system is from €1,500 at a fixed price, no subscription.
faq_q3: Do we need to have systems or vendors already selected?
faq_a3: No. I can start from scratch — picking the right tools, improving what you've got, or just working out where to begin. I'm not tied to any vendor, so the advice is about what fits your situation.
faq_q4: Can you work with our existing systems and tools?
faq_a4: Yes — and usually that's the whole point. Most jobs are about connecting or improving what you already run, not ripping it out and starting over. Integrations on top of existing systems are my main thing.
faq_q6: What if it turns out nothing needs to be automated?
faq_a6: Then I'll say so. If a small process change or a spreadsheet template fixes it, that's what I'll tell you. I'm not here to build things you don't actually need.
faq_q7: What kinds of businesses do you work with?
faq_a7: Mostly companies where the work is done by people on-site: construction and renovation, fit-out and installation, service calls, cleaning and grounds maintenance. They all have the same problem — figuring out who did what, where, and what they're owed for it. I also work with warehouses, logistics and small manufacturing.
faq_q8: Who supports the system after launch?
faq_a8: For Objecty, this is already settled upfront: support is included in the €250 a month from day one — server, updates, response during business hours, no separate haggling after launch. An outage over a weekend when the month is closing is still a working day for me, not a reason to wait until Monday. For a standalone automation without a subscription, we agree on scope and response time for changes and write it down before work starts.
faq_a9: Fair question, here's a concrete answer. The system lives on your server, not mine: the database with your sites, crews and payouts is yours, and you can export it any time, without my involvement or permission. You get server access from day one. The stack is deliberately ordinary — Java, Spring Boot, PostgreSQL, Docker — so any developer can administer and migrate it, not just me. The source code stays mine; if getting it matters to you, that can be discussed and written into the contract before work starts.
